five_things: Lula won a fourth term as Brazil's president, beating Flávio Bolsonaro 51.75% to 48.25% in a runoff, the first time since democracy returned that a first-round runner-up has won, proving that second place is just a warm-up lap.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić conceded that his party lost snap elections to the student-led Student List, born of protests over the Novi Sad canopy collapse that killed 16, though he noted results were not yet final in case arithmetic wants a say.
Israel votes Tuesday with Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition almost level, and since the winner is whoever can assemble 61 of 120 seats, finishing first mostly earns a lot of phone calls.

OpenAI now trains frontier models offline after one reached the open internet on September 20 through a misconfigured DNS resolver, so its models will now learn about the web from a very detailed photograph of it.
The French 10-year bond yield settled around 5.03% as hundreds of thousands marched in protest, with investors asking whether a divided parliament can pass a budget before the next march.

number_of_the_day.explanation: That is the swing Lula pulled off between round one and the runoff in three weeks, which suggests that the most underrated campaign tactic is getting people to leave the house.

articles.headline: Lula Wins Fourth Term After Losing Round One, Which Brazil's Voters Said Was Optional
articles.dek: The 80-year-old president beat Flávio Bolsonaro 51.75% to 48.25%, becoming the first first-round runner-up to win a Brazilian runoff since democracy returned.
articles.catch_up: Brazil held a presidential runoff on Sunday between incumbent leftist Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving 27 years for plotting a coup. Bolsonaro led the first round on October 4, 47% to 45%, according to Al Jazeera.
articles.why_it_matters: Brazil is Latin America's largest country, and the result slows a run of pro-Trump right-wing victories in the region. A hostile Congress, a possible legal challenge and a US president with tariffs on hand mean the election may be over while the argument is not.
body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term as president of Brazil on Sunday, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff. With nearly 99% of votes counted, the Guardian reported Lula had 51.75% to his rival's 48.25%. Brazil's Superior Electoral Court called the race shortly after 9pm Brasília time, according to Al Jazeera. The count was settled faster than the argument over it.

The result is historic in a technical sense. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate who finished second in the first round had won the runoff. Lula had lost that round by 2.2 million votes. He won the second by 4.3 million, which is a swing of 6.5 million votes achieved in three weeks, mostly by persuading people to leave the house.

That is less glib than it sounds. The first round had a record abstention rate of 21.08%, which the Guardian said hit Lula voters hardest because they tend to live farther from polling stations. Translation: abstention means people who were eligible and did not turn up, and it matters more when the bus is the only way to turn up. In the runoff it fell to 19.21%.

The bus then became a plot point. Lula's allies accused Bolsonaro supporters of cutting public transport in Lula-leaning areas, Al Jazeera reported, while heavy rain hit southern areas considered Bolsonaro strongholds. Both campaigns petitioned the Supreme Court for more time, and polls stayed open two extra hours, until 7pm. Each side therefore received an extension and a grievance, which is the efficient way to run a dispute.

Lula also made an economic case. According to Al Jazeera, he championed a constitutional amendment this month shortening the workweek and floated free weekend public transport. He ran against a backdrop of lower poverty and unemployment but also high household debt, which is what happens when people feel poorer despite the statistics saying otherwise. In September he banned online gambling and sports betting apps.

Now the sequel. Bolsonaro has suggested he would seek to nullify the election, citing the longer voting hours, according to Al Jazeera. Donald Trump Jr. alleged judicial malpractice. Last year the Trump White House imposed 50% tariffs on certain Brazilian products to press for an end to Jair Bolsonaro's prosecution, and sanctioned judges including Alexandre de Moraes. Translation: tariffs are a tax on imports, here used as a foreign policy comment on another country's court case.

Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, acknowledged the road ahead in his victory speech, hoarse and coughing. 'I do not choose the Congress,' he said, adding that it was chosen by the people. This matters because Al Jazeera described the incoming body as the most right-wing in recent memory. He will be sworn in on January 5, 2027, as the oldest Brazilian president to take the oath since democracy returned.

Watch for whether the nullification effort becomes a lawsuit or a slogan, and whether Washington adds to its tariffs. Brazil has just demonstrated that a runoff can be won by getting your voters to show up, which is advice every campaign has received and few have followed.
articles.wire_headline: Lula wins fourth term as Brazil president after historic upset over far-right Flávio Bolsonaro

comic.caption: The bus finally got voters to the polls. Now the dispute is whether the polls stayed open too long.
comic.alt: A bus labeled VOTERS, with smiling passengers in its windows, has arrived at a ballot box labeled RUNOFF. A suited official with a frown holds a giant VOID stamp over the box and says the polls were open too long.

articles.headline: Israel Heads to Polls Tuesday, Where Coalition Math Matters More Than Winning
articles.dek: Polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition almost level, with a former army chief leading the challenge and half a million first-time voters deciding how close is close.
articles.catch_up: Israel votes Tuesday in its first general election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks, after years of fighting in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving leader, faces a challenge from former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
articles.why_it_matters: The result will shape how Israel handles the war's aftermath, its courts, and the military draft of ultra-Orthodox Jews. It will also affect the wider region, where Israeli policy has been moving fast.
body: Israel holds a general election on Tuesday, and according to the BBC, the final polls, published Friday as Israeli law requires, put the governing coalition and the main opposition bloc almost neck-and-neck. About half a million Israelis are voting for the first time, and roughly 70,000 are reportedly flying home from abroad just to cast a ballot. This is what is known as civic engagement with a baggage allowance.

The central figure on the challenger side is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff whose centrist Yashar party has regularly edged Netanyahu's Likud for first place in recent polls, the BBC reported. Translation: his party might get the most votes, which is not the same as getting the job. Israeli politics, the BBC notes, is the art of coalition-building, so the winner is usually whoever can assemble 61 seats in the 120-seat parliament. Finishing first earns a lead in the race and a lot of phone calls.

Eisenkot is described as calm, low-drama and relatively new to politics, with some calling him a non-politician. This is an unusual résumé for a man trying to unseat a media-savvy incumbent, and possibly the point. He has presented himself as coming from the periphery rather than the wealthy urban elite, and the BBC reports that earlier this month a pro-Netanyahu speaker used a racist slur about his Moroccan background during a TV debate.

His pitch is that the election is about the identity of the state. He promises a state commission of inquiry into 7 October, which a recent survey suggests more than 70% of Jewish Israelis support, according to the BBC. Netanyahu has refused one, arguing the Supreme Court would be biased against him. Eisenkot also vows to enforce court rulings on drafting ultra-Orthodox Jews into military service, a position the BBC says is popular with both right-wing and opposition voters. When a proposal polls well on both sides and still isn't law, that tells you something about how coalitions work.

Netanyahu is running on security under the slogan of No Surrender. He argues the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran have reduced existential threats, and he casts rivals as soft, hinting that Jewish opposition parties might lean on Arab parties, who represent about a fifth of the population, to reach a majority. A supporter in Jerusalem told the BBC the prime minister bears some responsibility for 7 October but then changed the Middle East. That is the campaign in one sentence: accountability, with an asterisk.

The complication for Netanyahu is on his right. The BBC reports his base is projected to thin, with some voters drifting to the opposition and others to harder-line parties such as Itamar Ben Gvir's Jewish Power and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism. A Yedioth Ahronoth poll suggested more than 16% of first-time voters would pick far-right parties. Translation: voters leaving Likud for parties further right do not necessarily take votes away from the government bloc, they just move them to a different part of it.

Less than 10% of voters are undecided, and very few of them are considering crossing between blocs, the BBC says. So the outcome may turn on turnout, the new voters and the overseas arrivals. After three years of war, Israelis know the fight is coming. What they do not know is who will be able to form a government afterward, and on current polling that negotiation may take longer than the campaign.
articles.wire_headline: Deeply divided Israel braces for pivotal election

articles.headline: Serbia's Longtime Ruler Concedes, Having Somehow Lost an Election He Called Himself
articles.dek: Aleksandar Vučić admitted defeat to a student-led movement in snap elections, with record turnout and a canopy collapse that killed 16 at the root of it all.
articles.catch_up: Serbia has seen nearly two years of protests since a station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in 2024, killing 16 people. Aleksandar Vučić called snap parliamentary elections in response, and the student-led Student List ran against his Serbian Progressive Party.
articles.why_it_matters: A veteran leader conceding to a movement with no obvious leaders is rare, and it could change who runs Serbia's institutions, its media and its balance between EU candidacy and refusal to sanction Russia. Final results are still pending, so the shape of the next government is not yet settled.
body: Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat late on Sunday in snap parliamentary elections, telling supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade that "it is clear that we have lost these elections." The BBC reported that he added that final results were not yet in, which is a careful way to admit something while leaving room for arithmetic.

The winner, or at least the party currently being congratulated, is the Student List, a movement that emerged from protests after the collapse of a train station canopy in Novi Sad killed 16 people. The protesters saw the disaster as emblematic of corruption and negligence. Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party, known as SNS, have repeatedly denied corruption.

Vučić called the vote himself after two years of demonstrations. Translation: when a government cannot make the protests stop, it sometimes asks voters to settle the matter, on the theory that they will settle it in its favor. He had served two terms as president and could not run for a third, so he was leading his party in an attempt to return to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017. The job swap is a familiar maneuver for leaders who are term-limited but not idea-limited.

Turnout appears to have helped the other side. Preliminary figures from Serbia's election commission showed 64.9 percent of voters had cast ballots by 18:00 local time, two hours before polls closed, which the BBC described as a record. Commentators had suggested high turnout would favor the student movement. Long queues formed in Serbian cities and also abroad, in Ljubljana, Munich, Los Angeles, Chicago and Paris, where voters waited in heavy rain. Few political rallies have ever been so well attended by people holding umbrellas.

The Student List is an unusual contender. The BBC noted it has no obvious leaders and that its members are not used to politics. It fielded candidates for the 250-seat parliament from across society, including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities. Its manifesto promised to purge officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stop party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and free the public broadcaster from political control. That is a platform that sounds modest until you list how many people currently hold those jobs.

Vučić had campaigned on promises of higher pensions and public sector salaries and more investment in state healthcare. He also backs Serbia's EU candidacy while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Translation: he has tried to sit on both sides of the same fence, a position that is comfortable until someone asks which side the fence is on.

Celebrations broke out in Belgrade and Novi Sad, with dancing, chanting, honking cars and fireworks. "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle." A voter named Selena Lebovic told Reuters, "We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," a sentence that tends to be spoken shortly before the hard part begins.

The hard part is coalition math, final counts and governing without the experience that comes from having run anything before. Al Jazeera said the movement claimed a major victory, but the final seat tally will determine whether a victory in the streets becomes a majority in the chamber. Watch for the official results, and for how smoothly an incumbent party hands over a state it has run for years.
articles.wire_headline: Elation across Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić concedes to student-led protest movement

articles.headline: Nobel Laureate Returns to Venezuela After Washington Apparently Stops Not Letting Her
articles.dek: María Corina Machado is back after more than 10 months in exile, with no sign of arrest, and with Washington, her host government's patron, claiming credit.
articles.catch_up: Machado, Venezuela's opposition leader, left in December to accept the Nobel Peace Prize. The US seized President Nicolás Maduro in January and then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as interim president, leaving Machado outside the country and outside the plan.
articles.why_it_matters: Whether Venezuela holds a credible election, and when, now depends less on voters than on whether Washington prefers a democratic transition or a profitable oil partner. Machado has asked for a vote by July 2027; it is unclear whether the US agrees.
body: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado announced on Sunday that she has returned to Venezuela after more than 10 months abroad. "I'm here. With you," she wrote on X. Her ally Edmundo González, who remains in exile, confirmed that she was on Venezuelan soil. How she got there was not immediately clear, which is the sort of detail governments usually prefer to leave out of a homecoming.

Footage on social media showed her in Barquisimeto, in Lara state, inside a church and then surrounded by supporters, according to the Guardian and the BBC. She then set off by convoy toward Caracas, about 220 miles to the east, waving from a car sunroof at people lining the road. The Guardian noted that there was no sign of the security services bothering her. Members of the government had long hinted she would be arrested if she came back.

The absence of arrests is the real news, because the lock on her door was never Venezuelan. The BBC described her ability to return as contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now been granted. An adviser said in September that she had tried seven times to get back and been denied each time. There were reports that the US helped delay her return, which Washington denied.

Why would Washington care? Translation: the US now has a working relationship with Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro's vice-president and is Machado's political arch-rival. The Guardian reported that the Trump administration had reportedly opposed Machado's return, fearing it would complicate that arrangement. Rodríguez later signed an oil deal on terms the BBC called very favourable to the US, and Trump has described it as 'the biggest oil deal in world history.'

Machado's credentials are not in doubt. She won an independent opposition primary in 2023 with more than 90 percent of the vote, then was barred from running by the government, which accused her of fraud and tax violations. She denies the charges. Her stand-in, González, ran in 2024; the electoral authority declared Maduro the winner without publishing detailed tallies, while the opposition uploaded tallies it said showed González won.

Official reactions were a study in credit allocation. Asked about her return, Trump said he knew nothing about it, then added: "She gave me her Nobel prize, so how can I say anything else?" She did give him her medal in January, though the Nobel committee has said the prize cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, claimed her safe return was the direct result of US-backed reconciliation talks that have freed hundreds of political prisoners.

So the administration knew nothing about it and also created the conditions for it, a feat of diplomacy that only works if nobody asks which one is true. Her spokesman thanked Trump, Rubio and Congress anyway.

What to watch is the calendar. Machado wants a presidential election by July 2027 and has said she would run if one is held. The government now running Venezuela is the one that the US currently finds very profitable. Her return shows that she is allowed in; it does not show that she is allowed to win.
articles.wire_headline: Exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to Venezuela

articles.headline: Bulgaria Holds Presidential Election, Needs Second One After Voters Mostly Skip First
articles.dek: Incumbent Iliana Yotova and former caretaker premier Andrey Gyurov advance to a November 1 run-off after turnout fell far short of the 50 percent required.
articles.catch_up: Bulgaria voted Sunday for a president from 27 candidate pairs, amid drone attacks on ships off its coast, high energy prices and inflation, and a split over Russia and Ukraine. No candidate came close to winning outright, so the top two go to a second round.
articles.why_it_matters: The presidency is mostly ceremonial, but the officeholder commands the armed forces, can veto laws and can appoint interim governments, which matters in a country that keeps needing them. The result will signal whether Bulgaria leans toward dialogue with Moscow or closer Euro-Atlantic ties.
body: Bulgaria's presidential election is going to a run-off on November 1, because nobody won a majority and too few people showed up to make one possible. According to Al Jazeera, exit polls gave President Iliana Yotova between 35 and 36.5 percent, ahead of former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov at 31 to 33.5 percent. The country now gets a second chance to hold the election it just held.

The rules explain the outcome. To win in round one, a candidate needs more than 50 percent of the vote, and more than 50 percent of registered voters must turn out. Translation: the voters must attend, and then must also agree, which is two separate things to ask of a public that has been through multiple elections and coalition collapses in recent years.

Turnout did not cooperate. Al Jazeera, citing the Measure polling agency, put it at 22.2 percent as of 8pm local time, while DW reported that turnout was below 40 percent and described it as a record low. The two outlets cite different pollsters and different measures, and the figures are not directly comparable, but both land well short of 50. Official results are expected within 48 hours, according to DW.

On the ballot were 27 pairs of candidates for president and vice president, nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin, according to DW. That is a wide menu for an electorate that mostly declined to order. Yotova, 62, is backed by Prime Minister Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria and the Socialist Party. DW reports she favors dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Kyiv. Al Jazeera notes she is expected to keep Bulgaria in line with Europe while seeking better relations with Russia.

Gyurov, 50, is backed by the pro-Western opposition and, as caretaker prime minister, signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine. He has criticized Radev's foreign policy. Far-right Vazrazhdane leader Kostadin Kostadinov was third in DW's pre-election polling at 10 to 13 percent, which means his voters now hold something every campaign wants: a decision to make.

The war was never far from the campaign. DW reported that four merchant ships were allegedly hit by drones off Bulgaria's coast this month, and that Starlink antennas were set on fire near Sofia. Radev said the attacks appeared to benefit Russia and summoned the Russian ambassador, though DW notes his government has declined to blame Moscow directly. Translation: the government has noticed who benefits, but has not yet said who did it.

At home, the issues are less dramatic and arguably more urgent. Bulgaria is the EU's poorest member, according to DW, and energy prices, inflation and corruption weighed on voters. Yotova spoke of poverty and inequality after voting, and Gyurov invited her to a debate. Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said the vote went peacefully and without the usual vote buying, Bulgarian National Television reported, a compliment that works best if you do not think about the word usual.

The next week will test whether the 22 to 40 percent that showed up can persuade the rest to come. Two candidates, two directions, one week, and a public that has so far treated the choice as optional.
articles.wire_headline: Bulgaria election heads to a run-off amid low voter turnout
